We're sharing the story of YUI, the first animated short film made with Comfy Agent, by one of the best AI animation artists 852話 Hakoniwa. And she also made YUI tell her own behind-the-scenes story!

Hakoniwa has been supporting the Comfy community. Today, 70% of her work is generated through ComfyUI. I got to know Hakoniwa in 2023 and we were both just ComfyUI open-source users back then. Then we worked together in the CCS New Art Manifesto exhibition in Tokyo.

She was the first artist who tried out Comfy Agent. She worked day and night on it, because this was the story she had always wanted to create. It was so much fun creating together. We chose the look for YUI with love.

YUI's story is also her story. The creation will never end. I hope you all enjoy the 2 videos!

posts.description:
This launch video wasn't made by a studio. It was generated by an AI agent running Kimi K3 and Hyperframe, in about 40 minutes end to end.
No editor. No After Effects. No stock library. Attached below, completely unedited.
What the agent actually shipped:
A 28 second, 1080p launch film for ReplicaVox.
8 animated scenes. Kinetic type, a live reconstruction of our own product UI, stat counters, a voice clone morph, an original generated score, 13 sound effects placed on the beats.
Every frame written as real code. Nothing templated.
Now the part that should matter to founders.
I never gave it a brand guide. The agent went to our live website and extracted the brand itself. Our fonts. Our violet. Our actual product interface. It studied a reference video I liked, designed its own visual language, then reviewed its own frames and re-rendered what wasn't good enough.
It didn't just execute. It made taste calls. Good ones.
One model did the research, design, motion, music, QC and final render. All of it running on Kimi K3, whose 1M token context let the agent hold the brief, the brand system, all 8 scenes and its own QA notes in a single conversation.
For years the question founders asked was "who do we hire for this."
The cost of production just fell to the price of a conversation. What's left to compete on is taste, speed and distribution. That's the actual shift.
And because talk is cheap, the entire project is public in HyperFrames. Open it, remix it, make your own launch film:
https://lnkd.in/dBSdhYXt
Try picking a weak frame in the video below. I'll wait.
#KimiK3 #MoonshotAI #HyperFrames #AIAgents #GenerativeAI #ReplicaVox #BuildInPublic

posts.description:
We premiered our AI animated film at the world's biggest computer graphics conference:

Kök Börü a 15-minute historical drama, set in 15th-century Central Asia, following a nomadic mother searching for a daughter lost to a wolf pack.

A folklore film like this normally takes one to two years and $1-2M. We made it with a team of 12 in 2 weeks, on a process built around artists:

→ Characters and environments were generated on Higgsfield AI
→ Artists drew and painted over them by hand
→ Those drawings guided every shot the AI produced
→ Real actors were filmed and mapped onto the characters
→ Native actors gave the characters their voices

Directors and animators made every real creative choice from start to finish, with the AI following their work along the way. That's how the tools should work: giving creators the reach to make films that would never have gotten funded otherwise.

Huge credit to directors Shakhnazar Borboev, Amina Umirzhanova, and Stepan Abramov for putting a story from their homeland on the SIGGRAPH 2026 stage in LA alongside Pixar, Disney, and Nvidia.

We've made everything behind this project public. Every prompt and every asset is now free to study and use.

Check out full workflow here: https://lnkd.in/ez_VDWPt

posts.description:
Excited to share our latest film, Le Drip — made with Ezra Li and based on an original story by Jessie Hughes.

Watch it here: https://lnkd.in/gMX5JXNG

Ezra and I met during the Google Flow Sessions residency and immediately hit it off. When I showed him the crappy silent animatic I'd made for this film, he started riffing a hilarious inner monologue of an old French man. I knew right then he had to write the script... and that's how we ended up with this lovely existential painterly French animation.

I'm really proud of the bespoke stop-motion quality we were able to achieve in this film. With previous models, this was extremely hard to do consistently. But once Seedance 2.0 dropped and we tried a few shots with it, it was to both my horror and delight just how good the prompt adherence had become. The painful part was deciding if all 70 shots in the film should be redone. We just said 'fuck it' and redid all 70 in one weekend. 🙃 Luckily, because I had built the procedural workflows in FLORA, the process of replacing the shots was actually a lot less painful than it seemed from the outset.

Inside Flora, we used Google's Nano Banana for image generation, Claude for prompt iteration, and ByteDance's Seedance 2.0 for video generation. Runway handled storyboarding and additional video. Adobe was used for video and sound, and Leonardo.Ai for additional video. A custom typography tool built in Google AI Studio animated the closing credits in a handmade stop-motion style that matches the film's painterly aesthetic. ElevenLabs handled voice transformation and selected sound effects.

More BTS coming soon.

Special thanks to all the Creative Partner Programs that helped make this film possible: FLORA, Adobe, Runway, Google, and Leonardo.Ai.

And of course, it wouldn't have been possible without all these wonderful humans who helped bring the sound, color, story and soul of the film to life:

posts.description:
I had a slide I knew would lose the room. So I turned it into a one-minute animated video with Claude Opus 5.5! I wanted to share it so you can try it too.

What surprised me is that Claude cannot generate video directly, but it can write the whole animation as code and turn it into a video file. It also understood what I was describing better than any other model I use, and it was really good at bringing together what I had in my head.

Until now I would have gone to a video generation model for something like this. This time I worked with Claude, and after a few rounds we got to the version you see here.

A few of the keywords I used, in case they give you ideas
- 2D illustration, cute characters, hand-drawn explainer style
- pop-up text coming in from the sides
- neutral story, no judgement between old and new
- retro-futuristic, 1960s space age colours, halftone texture
- old TV static
- animate it in code and export as MP4

Then I added my own layers. I generated the narration from text in ElevenLabs with an old radio effect, created a background track in Suno to match the vintage feel, used ChatGPT for one of the illustrations, and put it all together in Capcut. All took a couple of hours.

This is how I like to work: I start from what I need, think about what each tool does best, and connect them.

Which part of your work could become a short explainer like this?

Anthropic #claude

posts.description:
AI animation is reaching a point where people are watching clips like this without realizing they were made with AI.

“Smooth Operator” by @antrofrog follows one very calm man walking through London with a coffee and umbrella, casually fixing everything around him without ever breaking stride.

He catches a flying hat, saves a kid on a runaway scooter, returns stolen sausages to a butcher, rescues a cat, catches a falling ice cream and stops a purse thief.

Then a taxi sends a wall of water toward him, and he spins the umbrella fast enough to block it.

All while Sade’s “Smooth Operator” plays in the background.

The clip went viral in part because viewers said they thought they were watching a normal animated short before certain scenes gave away that it was AI.

That may be the most interesting part. AI animation is getting good enough that the first question is starting to shift from “does this look like AI?” to “when do you notice?”

posts.description:
I spent my entire Sunday last weekend, from morning until 1:30 AM, making an AI animated short film. It cost me around $80 and a lot of re-generations, and I am completely blown away by how it turned out.

Here is how I built it. I used Higgsfield AI as the main platform, with Nano Banana Pro for all the images. I created character sheets, locations, and different visual styles for the different realities and universes inside the story.

For the video generation, I used Seedance 2.0 video generation model.

Most of the day actually went into learning. Keeping the character consistent across scenes, experimenting with different animation and cartoon styles, and figuring out how to get good output by feeding the models the right references.

Video regenerations are not cheap, so the cost added up quickly. But the learning was the whole point.

What struck me most is where these tools are right now. Remember how coding agents hit their inflection point around November 2025, and suddenly Claude Code was everywhere and everyone was using it for coding and a lot more.

I think image and video models are having that same moment. Nano Banana was a big inflection point for images last year, and Seedance 2.0 feels like the same kind of leap for video this year.

Right now these two feel best-in-class to me. I had tried making something like this a few months ago and it did not come out well at all. This time the result genuinely surprised me.

On a personal note, I have loved cartoons since I was a kid, and making my own has always been a dream of mine. What excites me is that you no longer need formal animation training or years of practice to make something that is actually good. The models have reached that point.

If you have a story to tell, tools like these are a fantastic way to tell it in a format that grabs attention and is easy for anyone to consume. Whether that is your product, your service, or just a short film for the fun of it.

For the record, this is not sponsored in any way. I am simply becoming a fan of Higgsfield. If you have some time and a bit of money to throw, give animated short film making a try. I think it might blow your mind too.

Check out the 2-minute Animated Short file that I made. Let me know what you think in the comments 😁

posts.description:
If you have not watched this short film that combines great human talent with the possibilities of AI you should.

This is the current state of the art of the possible combining human script, voice, creative decisioning with the possibilities of AI technology

The short film Pomegranate utilized AI for all visual elements, including shot generation via Midjourney v7 and animation through Kling, while real human actors provided the voices and a Foley artist managed the sound design. This hybrid approach allowed for a visually consistent sci-fi universe supported by traditional human artistry in writing, directing, and musical composition.Less

To further distinguish between the technological and human contributions in Pomegranate, here is a detailed breakdown of the production:

What was AI-Generated?

The film's visual identity was almost entirely driven by AI tools:

Visual Concepts: Every shot began as a still image generated by Midjourney v7.
Animation: Static images were animated using Kling and Nano Banana to create fluid motion and character movement.

Lip-Syncing: Tools like Sync Labs were used to match the AI-generated characters' mouths to the recorded human dialogue.

World Building: The film is noted for using AI to maintain a consistent aesthetic across its 30-minute runtime, a challenge in earlier AI video efforts.

What was "Live" (Human)?

Director Zack London (known as Gossip Goblin) maintains that AI is a "force multiplier" rather than a replacement for human intent:

Voice Acting: The film relies on a human voice cast, including a lead actor London discovered in Sweden. The director specifically avoided AI voices to ensure emotional resonance.

Sound and Music: The film features paid composers and a Foley artist for sound effects, ensuring the audio landscape was crafted by hand.

Direction and Script: The story, lore, and script were written by humans. The director describes the process as imagined and directed by people, with AI serving as the "camera" and "set."

Editing: Standard film techniques, such as J and L cuts, were applied by a human editor to pace the dialogue and scenes.

While some viewers initially mistook the film's simulated reality themes—where characters use "spools" to live virtual lives—as a description of the AI production itself, the "live" elements refer to the tangible human performances and technical crafts behind the screen.

By Gossip Goblin aka Zach London and colleagues

comments.text: "Human creativity leads. Writing, design, performance, direction, and cinematography are human-driven. Filmmakers set the vision and drive the creative choices. AI is a tool that frees creators to focus on craft." Love this. It's the same principle that we adopted several months ago when we started developing our 8-year-old granddaughter's animated series. She is the driving force behind it and has full creative control over all elements. She creates the stories using 2D mockups, and I record her. Then I write the script based on the recording. She then sits with me to read and approve the final draft. One very memorable moment was when she stopped me while we read the script. "Wait... Papa, you can't use that word, Spy. Little kids don't know what that word means yet. You need to change it to: LUCY'S MOM: We need to keep an eye on her without her seeing us when she goes out to the garden." Yes, she was right. Little kids will understand that wording. That's why she has the final word on everything. As far as consistency with characters, we created "Pose Packs" for every character and use Photoshop to create each scene and develop the storyboard. She approves the storyboard before motion is applied.
comments.author: John Washco

comments.text:
Well said, Albert. Your “it takes a village of artists and scientists” approach to AI filmmaking is 🔥!

Circus of Want is editing two AI-assisted vertical series—it’s been an eye-opening journey from render one. We use AI alongside Photoshop, Premiere Pro, and After Effects to bring our 100% human-written stories to life.

Thru creative direction and strategic editing, we’re battling the drift beast—character, prop, and world inconsistencies that creep into AI-generated shots. The downside? Wrestling that beast adds costly revisions and project delays.

On the upside, we’re developing workflow tools to tackle these issues and help other studios do the same. Looking forward to the day when taming the drift monster takes less time than telling the story.
